title: Liouville theorem
section: Complex Variables ▷ Theorems Concerning Analytic Functions
terms: Liouville theorem; bounded entire function; fundamental theorem of algebra via analysis.

exposition.text:
Liouville’s theorem says that every bounded entire function is constant. It follows from
Cauchy’s estimate for the first derivative by sending the radius to infinity. Entire is essential:
nonconstant bounded holomorphic functions exist on the unit disk.
A useful strategy is to transform an unbounded-looking entire function into a bounded one.
For example an entire function bounded away from zero has bounded entire reciprocal and is
constant. Liouville also proves the fundamental theorem of algebra: a nonconstant polynomial
with no zero would have a bounded entire reciprocal.
A bounded holomorphic function on a punctured disk extends across its center by the
removable-singularity theorem. Thus a globally bounded holomorphic function on the punc-
tured plane is also constant, after extension. On a disk, by contrast, f(z) = z is bounded and
nonconstant.

question.text:
An entire function satisfies |f(z)| ≥ 2 for every z ∈ C. Which must be true?
(A) f is constant. (B) f(z) = 2 everywhere.
(C) f is linear. (D) f has a zero.
(E) f is unbounded.

solution.text:
The reciprocal 1/f is entire and bounded by 1/2, so is constant by Liouville. It is nonzero,
hence f itself is constant; its value need not equal 2.

question.text:
In a proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra, assume a nonconstant complex polynomial P
has no zero. Why is 1/P bounded on the entire plane?
(A) Every entire function is bounded.
(B) Because 1/P tends to zero at infinity and is continuous on each fixed closed disk.
(C) Because every polynomial has bounded modulus.
(D) Because |P (z)| ≥ 1 for every z.
(E) Because every nonzero complex number has modulus at least one.

solution.text:
The leading term gives |P(z)| → ∞ as |z| → ∞, so 1/P is bounded outside a sufficiently
large disk. The no-zero assumption makes 1/P continuous on the remaining compact disk,
where it has a finite maximum modulus. It is also entire. Liouville would make it constant,
contradicting the positive degree of P .

question.text:
For which of the following domains must every bounded holomorphic function be constant? I.
C; II. C \ {0}; III. {z : |z| < 1}.
(A) I only (B) II only (C) I and II only (D) I and III only (E) I, II, and III

solution.text:
I is Liouville's theorem. For II, boundedness near the isolated missing point makes it re-
movable; extending there gives a bounded entire function, again constant. For III, f(z) = z
is bounded and nonconstant. The puncture case needs the removable-singularity step, not
an unsupported application of Liouville to a proper domain.

question.text:
Which pair of entire functions shows that f(z)g(z) = 1 does not force either function to be
constant?
(A) f(z) = z, g(z) = 1/z
(B) f(z) = sin z, g(z) = 1/ sin z
z −z
(C) f(z) = e , g(z) = e
(D) f(z) = z + 1, g(z) = 1/(z + 1)
(E) f(z) = cos z, g(z) = 1/cos z

solution.text:
Both exponentials are entire, nonconstant, and nowhere zero, with product one. In each
other pair the reciprocal has a pole, so it is not entire. Liouville requires boundedness, not
merely absence of zeros.
